Hafez al-Assad. The dictator of Syria for twenty-nine years, ruling through the Ba'athist Party with iron-fisted authoritarianism. Assad became defense minister in nineteen sixty-six and consolidated power through a nineteen seventy coup d'état, ruling as president from nineteen seventy-one until his death in the year two thousand. He led Syria into the Yom Kippur War in nineteen seventy-three alongside Egypt against Israel; though the war ended in a military stalemate, it revived Syrian prestige. Assad maintained a repressive secret police apparatus called the Mukhabarat that suppressed dissent throughout his reign. In nineteen eighty-two, he crushed the Muslim Brotherhood in the city of Hama in a massacre killing tens of thousands. He intervened in Lebanon's civil war starting in nineteen seventy-six, stationing tens of thousands of troops to assert Syrian hegemony over the neighboring state for decades. Throughout the Cold War, he aligned with the Soviet Union, receiving military and economic aid while playing regional powerbroker. He promoted secular Arab nationalism through the Ba'athist Party's slogan Unity, Freedom, Socialism, despite the party's actual authoritarianism. When he died in June the year two thousand, his son Bashar al-Assad succeeded him, continuing the family dictatorship into the twenty-first century while remaining central to Middle Eastern geopolitics.
